newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Orange pips forecasts, branches out.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Orange pips forecasts, branches out.

text.p: Orange, Britain's youngest mobile telephone company, beat forecasts on Thursday by slashing half year pre-tax losses by 41 percent and said it was developing a host of advanced new services.

Orange, which expects to break into a pre-tax profit in the first half of 1999, said first half pre-tax losses narrowed to 74 million pounds ($117.4 million) -- about 15 percent above most analysts' expectations.
Helped by the growing popularity of its network and a 13 percent rise in annual revenues from each subscriber to 500 pounds, Orange broke into the black for the first time on an EBIDTA level.
Earnings before interest, depreciation, tax and amortisation came in at 12 million pounds compared to a 70 million pound loss in the first half of 1996.

Orange, which plans the new services to help win new customers and hold onto old ones, is Britain's third biggest mobile telephone company. An aggressive marketing campaign has won the digital operator more than one million customers and a 13.3 percent market share.

Finance director Graham Howe said Orange was "poised to set the agenda for the wirefree future" by developing new services such as Internet browsing, home shopping, on-line financial services, narrow-band TV, virtual banking and video telephony -- all via its handsets.

In order to be able to offer the services, Orange is doubling both the strength and planned investments in its network over the next 18 months. It plans to spend 800 million pounds on the national network by end-1999.
Orange will be using the headroom in its 1.2 billion pound debt facility, taken out in 1995, to fund the investment and will be looking to refinance the facility soon, Howe said.

Although Orange's shares jumped 10p to 222p on Thursday morning, some analysts warn that Orange might not be able to sustain its progress at the current rate and question whether future growth will be able to generate sufficient returns to justify the share price.
Orange's three rivals, who were caught off guard by their new rival's marketing campaign, are also starting to commit equally large sums to advertising.

Vodafone Group Plc, the market leader, has closed its high-street shops to Orange telephones. With the arrival of dual-band handsets, which work on two frequencies, some analysts also warn that Orange's low level of churn -- the number of customers switching operators or being cut off -- is bound to rise.

But Howe, who said Orange planned to reduce churn further, brushed off these suggestions -- and similar ones that the market is ripe for a fresh round of sharp price cuts to help boost sluggish British penetration levels of around 13 percent.
He sees a future where Orange will take on fixed-line giants such as British Telecommunications Plc and Cable and Wireless Communications .

"There's no reason why virtually 100 percent of the adult population at some point in the future will communicate through a mobile device," he said. "...There is no reason why you should rely on a wire in the wall."
Analyst forecasts that mobile penetration in Britain will rise to Scandinavian levels of 30 percent by 2006 are too conservative, he says -- despite current prices.
Having won a licence as part of a consortium to operate digital services in Austria, analysts expect Orange to look at similar opportunities in the Netherlands and Belgium. ($ = 0.630 British Pounds)
